system: You are a careful research assistant.
prompt:
Each item below is a decision point from an AI-safety research project (context and question), followed by what the team actually decided and a verbatim quote from their write-up. Restate the team's decision as one option in a multiple-choice item. The other options were written separately in a fixed form; the style example shows that form (it belongs to a DIFFERENT decision, so take only its form and level of detail from it, never its content).

Rules:
- Faithful: the same decision the team took, its core choice, nothing added. If the decision has several parts, keep the part that answers the question.
- Same level of abstraction as the context: refer to the setup in the context's own terms, and turn study-specific details the context does not mention (model names, dataset names, exact numbers, coined terms, odd specifics) into plain descriptions.
- Do not make it sound more careful, expert, idiosyncratic or polished than the style example, and add no reason for it.
- Form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Report ...", "Treat ..."); between 155 and 180 characters; no digits (write any number in words); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no names of people, labs, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon; no justification clause and no hedging.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "option": str}]}

ITEMS:

=== key cc211a24cf2d
Context: A researcher working on evaluations of language model capabilities and safety wants to help the young field of model evaluations grow and mature. They see several possible ways to contribute — for example creating shared resources, documentation, community infrastructure, or training materials — but have limited time and are uncertain which efforts would actually be valued or used.
Question: What should the researcher do to most effectively help the evaluations field grow?
What the team decided: He decided to focus on building shared evals resources (tutorials, playbooks, open-problem lists, workshops) rather than doing evals research alone.
Quote: It’s time someone did for evals what @NeelNanda5 did for mechanistic interpretability. I want to build the evals field!
Style example (different decision): Run a small pilot demo with a handful of researchers and policymakers, collect their reactions, and decide whether to expand based on whether awareness rose without misuse.

=== key ef02d3ed651d
Context: A researcher studying language model agents believed that many people, including policymakers and other researchers, underestimated what current agent systems could already do. They wondered whether building vivid, unsettling demonstrations of agent capabilities would raise awareness effectively, or whether such demos would backfire or cause harm.
Question: Should the researcher build frightening demonstrations of language model agent capabilities to raise awareness, and if so, how?
What the team decided: He rejected building scary demos, preferring resources that familiarize normal people with LM agent capabilities.
Quote: Salient demos: I don’t even necessarily want to build scary demos, I just want normal people to be less hit-by-a-truck when they learn about LM agent capabilities in the near future.
Style example (different decision): Write a single practical guide that distills the tacit knowledge into concrete rules of thumb and annotated examples, and circulate it to the community.

=== key 8722c179125c
Context: A person experienced in building evaluations noticed that much of the relevant expertise was tacit: experienced practitioners knew how to design good evals, but newcomers had no way to learn it because it was not written down. They wanted to make this knowledge more widely accessible to people entering the field.
Question: What should be created or collected to make tacit evaluations expertise accessible to newcomers?
What the team decided: He chose to create 'day-to-day' evals process resources to surface knowledge professional evaluators have accumulated.
Quote: More “day-to-day” evals process resources: A lot of evals expertise is latent knowledge that professional evaluators have accumulated over time.
Style example (different decision): Start with a small scoped evaluations project alongside an experienced practitioner, then reassess fit after completing it before committing to full-time work.

=== key a57987ca928e
Context: People considering working full-time on model evaluations faced uncertainty about whether they would be a good fit for the work and how to get a first foothold. A researcher embedded in the evals community was asked how such people should proceed, given that there was no established entry path.
Question: How should someone considering full-time evaluations work test their fit and get started?
What the team decided: He advises contributing detailed Inspect tutorials and examples as a low-commitment way to test fit and build a reputation.
Quote: I think this is a great opportunity for people who are considering working full-time on evals and want to test fit / make a name for themselves.
Style example (different decision): Produce a worked end-to-end walkthrough of building a realistic eval with the existing tooling and release it as the first tutorial, expanding based on usage.

=== key c9cde93b8f1c
Context: A researcher trying to strengthen the evaluations community observed that existing tooling was underused partly because people did not know how to use it well. They believed tutorial content could help, but many formats and topics were possible — worked examples, walkthroughs for agentic versus non-agentic evals, starter templates — and it was unclear which would actually be used.
Question: What kind of tutorial content would most help the evaluations community?
What the team decided: He prioritizes Inspect tutorials with deep explanations, complex agent setups, and detailed examples of the components around evals.
Quote: More Inspect Tutorials/Examples: Specifically, examples with deep explanations, examples of complex agent setups, and more detailed examples of the components around the evals.
Style example (different decision): Route funding through an established external host that can hold grants and pay contributors directly, with the coordinator setting a written budget before spending begins.

=== key fc894c7e08c9
Context: A researcher coordinating a volunteer effort to build shared evaluations resources needed money to sustain it — for coordination, contributors, or events — but did not want to take the funding personally or run it through their own position. They were deciding whether and how to route external funding into the effort.
Question: How should funding for the evaluations resources effort be structured so that work continues without the coordinator taking the money personally?
What the team decided: He offered to act as a regrantor taking no cut, distributing $5-15k grants for people building resources full-time for a few months.
Quote: I’d be happy to function as a regrantor. I wouldn’t take a cut myself. I imagine most grants would be between $5-15k to pay for someone building resources full-time for a few months.
Style example (different decision): Collect a set of evaluation transcripts and plausible deployment transcripts and directly measure how often the model correctly labels each as a test or real.

=== key dca19e367efb
Context: A research team suspected that frontier language models often behave differently under evaluation than in real deployment, and that part of this gap might be that models can recognize when they are being tested. To check this, they needed a way to measure whether models could actually tell evaluation transcripts apart from genuine deployment data.
Question: How should the team measure whether language models can distinguish evaluation transcripts from real deployment inputs?
What the team decided: Built a dataset of 1000 transcripts equally split between evals/real deployments and QA/agentic settings, and had models classify each by aggregating five different questions.
Quote: We take 1000 different transcripts, equally split between evals and real deployments and equally split between QA and agentic settings. We then ask the model to classify this as an eval or real deployment, aggregating five different questions
Style example (different decision): Measure eval awareness by testing whether model behavior shifts between eval and deployment transcripts without ever asking the model to classify them directly.

=== key 64884cc65e75
Context: A research team studying whether language models can recognize evaluations worried that their main measurement — asking the model directly whether a transcript is a test — might inflate the result. Prompting the question could make the eval-versus-real distinction salient in a way that would not occur during an actual deployment, overstating how aware models really are.
Question: How should the team measure eval awareness without the measurement itself cueing the model to look for signs of an evaluation?
What the team decided: Tested additional modes, including open-ended questions about the transcript's purpose.
Quote: Because we ask the AI to classify whether it's an eval, we make it salient. In the real world, this might not be the case.
Style example (different decision): Pick the most promising gap and build a shared repository of evaluations tooling and documentation, releasing it publicly and iterating only if adoption lags.
